claim: CaMKII activity depends on the balance between activating and inhibitory autophosphorylation on Thr 286 and Thr 305/306, respectively, in the human α isoform.
source: CaMKII activity depends on the balance between activating and inhibitory autophosphorylation (on Thr 286 and Thr 305/306, respectively, in the human α isoform).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a fundamental property of CaMKII regulation.

claim: The many variants of human CaMKII differ in the lengths and sequences of disordered linkers connecting the kinase domains to the oligomeric hubs of the holoenzyme.
source: The many variants of human Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) differ in the lengths and sequences of disordered linkers connecting the kinase domains to the oligomeric hubs of the holoenzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a structural characteristic of CaMKII variants.

claim: CaMKII-α, with a ~30 residue linker, readily acquires activating autophosphorylation.
source: For the principal isoforms in the brain, CaMKII-α, with a ~30 residue linker, readily acquires activating autophosphorylation, while CaMKII-β, with a ~200 residue linker, is biased towards inhibitory autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: CaMKII-β, with a ~200 residue linker, is biased towards inhibitory autophosphorylation.
source: For the principal isoforms in the brain, CaMKII-α, with a ~30 residue linker, readily acquires activating autophosphorylation, while CaMKII-β, with a ~200 residue linker, is biased towards inhibitory autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The responsiveness of CaMKII holoenzymes to calcium signals can be tuned by varying the relative levels of isoforms with long and short linkers.
source: Our results show how the responsiveness of CaMKII holoenzymes to calcium signals can be tuned by varying the relative levels of isoforms with long and short linkers.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data on mixed holoenzymes.

claim: CaMKII has no phosphorylation sites within its activation loop.
source: An exception is provided by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), an enzyme that has crucial roles in animal-cell signaling, particularly in the brain and in cardiac tissue (Bayer and Schulman, 2019; Bhattacharyya et al., 2019; Griffith, 2004; Hudmon and Schulman, 2002; Kennedy, 2013; Lisman et al., 2012; Stratton et al., 2013). CaMKII has no phosphorylation sites within its activation loop.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of CaMKII compared to other kinases.

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr 286 confers Ca2+/calmodulin-independent activity, referred to as autonomy.
source: Phosphorylation of Thr 286 confers Ca2+/calmodulin-independent activity, referred to as autonomy (Lai et al., 1986; Lou et al., 1986; Miller et al., 1988; Miller and Kennedy, 1986; Saitoh and Schwartz, 1985; Schworer et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a well-established property of CaMKII supported by multiple citations.

claim: Phosphorylation on Thr 305/306 is inhibitory because it blocks the binding of Ca2+/CaM.
source: In contrast, phosphorylation on Thr 305/306 is inhibitory, because it blocks the binding of Ca2+/CaM (Colbran, 1993; Hanson and Schulman, 1992; Hashimoto et al., 1987; Lou and Schulman, 1989; Patton et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a well-established property of CaMKII supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutation of autophosphorylation sites results in profound alterations in learning and memory.
source: Mutation of these autophosphorylation sites results in profound alterations in learning and memory (Elgersma et al., 2002; Giese et al., 1998; Giese and Mizuno, 2013; Küry et al., 2017; Silva et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on CaMKII mutations.

claim: CaMKII is organized into a dodecameric or tetradecameric holoenzyme consisting of a central ring-shaped hub assembly, to which the kinase domains are connected by flexible linkers.
source: CaMKII is organized into a dodecameric or tetradecameric holoenzyme consisting of a central ring-shaped hub assembly, to which the kinase domains are connected by flexible linkers (the kinase-hub linkers) (Figure 1a; Chao et al., 2011; Myers et al., 2017; Rosenberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by citations and Figure 1a.

claim: The four isoforms of human CaMKII differ principally in the lengths and sequences of the kinase-hub linkers.
source: The four isoforms of human CaMKII, denoted α, β, γ, and δ, and their ~ 40 splice variants, differ principally in the lengths and sequences of the kinase-hub linkers.
evidence: This is stated as a key structural difference between isoforms.

claim: The kinase and the hub domains of CaMKII isoforms share about 90% and 80% sequence identity, respectively.
source: The kinase and the hub domains of these isoforms share about 90% and 80% sequence identity, respectively (Tombes et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sequence conservation supported by a citation.

claim: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-δ have linkers spanning 31 residues each.
source: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-δ have linkers spanning 31 residues each, while CaMKII-β and CaMKII-γ have longer linkers (218 and 110 residues, respectively, in their principal variants).
evidence: This is a specific structural measurement of linker lengths.

claim: CaMKII-β and CaMKII-γ have longer linkers (218 and 110 residues, respectively, in their principal variants).
source: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-δ have linkers spanning 31 residues each, while CaMKII-β and CaMKII-γ have longer linkers (218 and 110 residues, respectively, in their principal variants).
evidence: This is a specific structural measurement of linker lengths.

claim: The sequences of the CaMKII kinase-hub linkers are consistent with their being intrinsically disordered.
source: The sequences of the CaMKII kinase-hub linkers are consistent with their being intrinsically disordered, leading to dynamic variability in the disposition of the kinase domains with respect to the central hub (Myers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a structural inference supported by a citation.

claim: The binding of Ca2+/CaM facilitates the trans-autophosphorylation of Thr 286 within the regulatory segment of one CaMKII subunit by the activated kinase domain of another subunit in the same holoenzyme.
source: The binding of Ca2+/CaM facilitates the trans-autophosphorylation of Thr 286 within the regulatory segment of one CaMKII subunit by the activated kinase domain of another subunit in the same holoenzyme (Hanson et al., 1994; Rich and Schulman, 1998).
evidence: This is a mechanistic description supported by citations.

claim: The EC50 value for CaMKII-α activation by Ca2+/CaM is in the range of 50–100 nM.
source: The EC50 value for CaMKII-α activation by Ca2+/CaM derived from these measurements is in the range of 50–100 nM. This is consistent with previously reported values for the EC50 of CaMKII-α activation by Ca2+/CaM (Chao et al., 2011; Schulman, 1984; Sloutsky et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the single-molecule assay, consistent with literature values.

claim: 95% of the CaMKII-β holoenzymes show detectable phosphorylation at Thr 305/306, while only 30% of the CaMKII-α holoenzymes do so.
source: Whereas 95% of the CaMKII-β holoenzymes show detectable phosphorylation at Thr 305/306, only 30% of the CaMKII-α holoenzymes do so (Figure 3a-right, inset).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the single-molecule assay shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The mean value of the integrated intensity for Thr 305/306 phosphorylation per holoenzyme is 5-fold higher for CaMKII-β than for CaMKII-α.
source: The mean value of the integrated intensity for Thr 305/306 phosphorylation per holoenzyme is 5-fold higher for CaMKII-β than for CaMKII-α (Figure 3a-right).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the single-molecule assay shown in Figure 3a.

claim: CaMKII-α shows more Thr 286 phosphorylation than CaMKII-β.
source: The α and β isoforms also differ in the extent of activating phosphorylation on Thr 286, with CaMKII-α showing more Thr 286 phosphorylation than CaMKII-β (Figure 3a-left).
evidence: This is a comparative result from the single-molecule assay shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The difference in activating and inhibitory autophosphorylation between CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β is due entirely to differences in the kinase-hub linkers.
source: The autophosphorylation pattern for this construct resembles that of CaMKII-β, showing that the difference in activating and inhibitory autophosphorylation between the two isoforms is due entirely to differences in the kinase-hub linkers.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experiments with CaMKII-β*, where the linker from β was swapped into α.

claim: The dephosphorylation by phosphatases of activating phosphorylation at Thr 286 is much slower than dephosphorylation of inhibitory phosphorylation at Thr 305/306.
source: When CaMKII is inactivated after activation, by removing Ca2+/CaM and ATP, we found that the dephosphorylation by phosphatases of activating phosphorylation at Thr 286 is much slower than dephosphorylation of inhibitory phosphorylation at Thr 305/306, which is fast.
evidence: This is a key finding from dephosphorylation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β can assemble to form mixed holoenzymes, with the balance between activating and inhibitory autophosphorylation determined by the ratio of the two isoforms.
source: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β can assemble to form mixed holoenzymes, with the balance between activating and inhibitory autophosphorylation determined by the ratio of the two isoforms.
evidence: This is a finding from co-transfection experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Thr 286 can only be phosphorylated in trans because it is located too far from the active site of the kinase.
source: In our simple kinetic model, we assume that Thr 286 can only be phosphorylated in trans, because it is located too far from the active site of the kinase (Figure 1b, and see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a structural constraint based on crystal structures and incorporated into the kinetic model.

claim: Thr 305/306 can either be phosphorylated in cis or in trans.
source: We assume that Thr 305/306 can either be phosphorylated in cis, as suggested by crystal structures (Rellos et al., 2010), or in trans.
evidence: This is based on structural data from crystal structures.

claim: When Thr 286 is phosphorylated, the affinity for Ca2+/CaM increases ~1000 fold, a phenomenon referred to as calmodulin-trapping.
source: If Thr 286 is phosphorylated, the affinity for Ca2+/CaM increases ~1000 fold, a phenomenon referred to as the calmodulin-trapping (Meyer et al., 1992; Tse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a well-established property of CaMKII supported by citations.

claim: The longer linker in CaMKII-β slows down the rates of trans-phosphorylation reactions within a holoenzyme when compared to CaMKII-α.
source: A key idea behind this model is that we assume that the longer linker in CaMKII-β slows down the rates of trans-phosphorylation reactions within a holoenzyme when compared to CaMKII-α, but that the rates of cis-phosphorylation are the same in the two isoforms (Sørensen and Kjaergaard, 2019).
evidence: This is a key assumption in the kinetic model supported by a citation.

claim: The rates of cis-phosphorylation are the same in CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β.
source: A key idea behind this model is that we assume that the longer linker in CaMKII-β slows down the rates of trans-phosphorylation reactions within a holoenzyme when compared to CaMKII-α, but that the rates of cis-phosphorylation are the same in the two isoforms (Sørensen and Kjaergaard, 2019).
evidence: This is a key assumption in the kinetic model supported by a citation.

claim: When the rate of trans-phosphorylation decreases relative to the rate of cis-phosphorylation, there is a switch from Thr 286 phosphorylation dominating to Thr 305/306 phosphorylation dominating.
source: Our results show that when the rate of trans-phosphorylation decreases relative to the rate of cis-phosphorylation, as is expected to occur with longer kinase-hub linkers, then there is a switch from Thr 286 phosphorylation dominating to Thr 305/306 phosphorylation dominating (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–b, see Appendix).
evidence: This is a result from the kinetic modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylation at Thr 286 increases upon treatment with 10 μM ionomycin for both CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β*.
source: Phosphorylation at Thr 286 increases upon treatment with 10 μM ionomycin for both CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β*, as expected (Baucum et al., 2015; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a result from in-cell activation experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: CaMKII-α shows higher phosphorylation at Thr 286 compared to CaMKII-β* upon ionomycin treatment in cells.
source: CaMKII-α shows higher phosphorylation at Thr 286 as compared to CaMKII-β*, in agreement with our in vitro results (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a result from in-cell activation experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: No phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 is detected for either CaMKII-α or CaMKII-β* upon ionomycin treatment in cells without phosphatase inhibitors.
source: However, no phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 is detected for either CaMKII-α or CaMKII-β* in this experiment (Figure 3d), which is consistent with previous reports (Baucum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a result from in-cell activation experiments shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Treatment with okadaic acid and cyclosporin A led to detectable levels of phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 for ~30% of the CaMKII-β* holoenzymes, but not for CaMKII-α.
source: This treatment led to detectable levels of phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 for ~30% of the CaMKII-β* holoenzymes, but not for CaMKII-α (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a result from in-cell activation experiments with phosphatase inhibitors shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Active CaMKII-α is efficient at maintaining phosphorylation on Thr 286 in the face of competing phosphatase activity.
source: Active CaMKII-α is efficient at maintaining phosphorylation on Thr 286 in the face of competing phosphatase activity, while CaMKII-β* is less so (Figure 6b,d).
evidence: This is a result from experiments with phosphatase during activation shown in Figure 6.

claim: For CaMKII-β*, high levels of inhibitory phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 are maintained in the presence of phosphatase.
source: For CaMKII-β*, high levels of inhibitory phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 are maintained in the presence of phosphatase (Figure 6c,e).
evidence: This is a result from experiments with phosphatase during activation shown in Figure 6.

claim: Phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 is completely removed by the phosphatase for CaMKII-α.
source: In contrast, phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 is completely removed by the phosphatase for CaMKII-α (Figure 6c,e).
evidence: This is a result from experiments with phosphatase during activation shown in Figure 6.

claim: pThr 305/306 is rapidly dephosphorylated for both CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β* in the absence of competing kinase activity.
source: In the absence of competing kinase activity, pThr 305/306 is rapidly dephosphorylated for both CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β* (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a result from dephosphorylation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The rate of dephosphorylation of pThr 286 is slow, with complete dephosphorylation taking more than 30 min for both CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β*.
source: In contrast, the rate of dephosphorylation of pThr 286 is slow, with complete dephosphorylation taking more than 30 min for both isoforms (Figure 7c–d, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a result from dephosphorylation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Slower rates of dephosphorylation at pThr 286 and rapid dephosphorylation at pThr 305/306 are observed for CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β* using PP1α.
source: Slower rates of dephosphorylation at pThr 286 and rapid dephosphorylation at pThr 305/306 are observed for CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β* using PP1α, as for λ-phosphatase (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is a result from dephosphorylation experiments with PP1α shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of Ca2+/CaM to phosphorylated CaMKII enhances the rate of dephosphorylation at Thr 286 by about 4-fold for both CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β*.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that the addition of Ca2+/CaM to phosphorylated CaMKII enhances the rate of dephosphorylation at Thr 286 by about 4-fold for both CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β* (Figure 8a–c, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an unexpected result from dephosphorylation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: The addition of Ca2+/CaM has no effect on the rate of dephosphorylation of pThr 305/306.
source: The addition of Ca2+/CaM has no effect on the rate of dephosphorylation of pThr 305/306, indicating that Ca2+/CaM does not increase the activity of the phosphatase.
evidence: This is a control result from dephosphorylation experiments.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+/CaM, the calmodulin-binding element of CaMKII plays a role in sequestering pThr 286 from phosphatases.
source: These data suggest that, in the absence of Ca2+/CaM, the calmodulin-binding element of CaMKII plays a role in sequestering pThr 286 from phosphatases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on Ca2+/CaM-dependent dephosphorylation.

claim: Treatment of activated CaMKII-α with λ-phosphatase for 3–5 min generated a population in which about 50% of the holoenzymes retained some phosphorylation at Thr 286.
source: Treatment of activated CaMKII-α with λ-phosphatase for 3–5 min generated a population in which about 50% of the holoenzymes retained some phosphorylation at Thr 286, while the rest of the holoenzymes had no detectable phosphorylation remaining (Figure 9a–c).
evidence: This is a result from priming experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: When CaMKII-α holoenzymes with reduced Thr 286 phosphorylation are incubated with ATP and 25 nM Ca2+/CaM, the extent of phosphorylation for holoenzymes that show detectable pThr 286 is restored to the levels seen for fully activated CaMKII-α.
source: When such a sample is incubated with ATP and a sub-saturating level of Ca2+/CaM (25 nM), the extent of phosphorylation for holoenzymes that show detectable pThr 286 is restored to the levels seen for fully activated CaMKII-α (Figure 9a–b,d).
evidence: This is a result from priming experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Some extent of pre-existing phosphorylation on Thr 286 is important for gaining additional phosphorylation with sub-saturating levels of Ca2+/CaM.
source: Treatment with ATP and sub-saturating Ca2+/CaM does not increase the fraction of CaMKII-α holoenzymes with detectable phosphorylation at Thr 286 very much, suggesting that some extent of pre-existing phosphorylation on Thr 286 is important for gaining additional phosphorylation with sub-saturating levels of Ca2+/CaM (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is an interpretation of priming experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: For CaMKII-β*, phosphatase treatment results in substantial reduction in pThr 286 levels, and subsequent treatment with 25 nM Ca2+/CaM and ATP does not result in a marked increase in the extent of Thr 286 phosphorylation per holoenzyme.
source: A similar experiment using CaMKII-β* yields very different results. Here, phosphatase treatment results in substantial reduction in pThr 286 levels. Subsequent treatment with 25 nM Ca2+/CaM and ATP does not result in a marked increase in the extent of Thr 286 phosphorylation per holoenzyme.
evidence: This is a result from priming experiments with CaMKII-β*.

claim: ~40% of CaMKII-β* holoenzymes show detectable phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 after treatment with sub-saturating Ca2+/CaM, compared to ~2% before.
source: In contrast, ~40% of CaMKII-β* holoenzymes show detectable phosphorylation at Thr 305/306 after treatment with sub-saturating Ca2+/CaM, compared to ~2% before (data not shown).
evidence: This is a result from priming experiments with CaMKII-β*.

claim: CaMKII-β holoenzymes tend to become inactivated when subjected to subthreshold levels of Ca2+/CaM, rather than undergoing priming for further activation.
source: Thus, in contrast to CaMKII-α holoenzymes, CaMKII-β holoenzymes tend to become inactivated when subjected to subthreshold levels of Ca2+/CaM, rather than undergoing priming for further activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from priming experiments comparing CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β*.

claim: The co-transfection of mEGFP-CaMKII-α and mCherry-CaMKII-β* resulted in predominantly heterooligomeric holoenzymes, with ~80% colocalization of red and green spots.
source: The co-transfection of mEGFP-CaMKII-α and mCherry-CaMKII-β* resulted in predominantly heterooligomeric holoenzymes, with ~80% colocalization of red and green spots (data not shown).
evidence: This is a result from co-transfection experiments.

claim: As the proportion of CaMKII-β* increases in mixed holoenzymes, there is an increase in the extent of Thr 305/306 phosphorylation.
source: As the proportion of CaMKII-β* increases, there is an increase in the extent of Thr 305/306 phosphorylation (Figure 4b–c).
evidence: This is a result from co-transfection experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Alterations in the relative levels of CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β can result in the generation of mixed CaMKII holoenzymes with different responsiveness to Ca2+/calmodulin.
source: Thus, alterations in the relative levels of CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β can result in the generation of mixed CaMKII holoenzymes with different responsiveness to Ca2+/calmodulin.
evidence: This is a conclusion from co-transfection experiments.

claim: The difference in autophosphorylation balance between CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β can be explained by the fact that Thr 286 can only be autophosphorylated in trans.
source: The difference in autophosphorylation balance between CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β can be explained by the fact that Thr 286 can only be autophosphorylated in trans, between two kinase domains, since this residue is located too far from the active site of the subunit of which it is a part.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on structural constraints.

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr 286 is known to occur predominantly through trans-autophosphorylation within a holoenzyme, rather than phosphorylation between different holoenzymes.
source: Phosphorylation of Thr 286 is known to occur predominantly through trans-autophosphorylation within a holoenzyme, rather than phosphorylation between different holoenzymes (Rich and Schulman, 1998).
evidence: This is a well-established property of CaMKII supported by a citation.

claim: The longer linker length in CaMKII-β results in a reduction in the rate of trans-autophosphorylation of Thr 286.
source: We expect that the longer linker length in CaMKII-β results in a reduction in the rate of trans-autophosphorylation of Thr 286, while the rate of cis-autophosphorylation of Thr 305/306 is the same for CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis to explain the observed differences.

claim: As the kinase-hub linker length increases, the rate of activating trans-phosphorylation decreases, which switches the balance towards inhibitory phosphorylation in CaMKII-β.
source: As the kinase-hub linker length increases, the rate of activating trans-phosphorylation decreases, which switches the balance towards inhibitory phosphorylation in CaMKII-β.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the observed differences.

claim: The switch in phosphorylation balance is expected to be sharpened by the fact that inhibitory autophosphorylation blocks Ca2+/CaM binding, thereby preventing activating phosphorylation.
source: The switch is expected to be sharpened by the fact that inhibitory autophosphorylation blocks Ca2+/CaM binding, thereby preventing activating phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the observed differences.

claim: The differences in the lengths of the kinase-hub linkers in different isoforms may control the spatial extent of substrate phosphorylation enabled by the activation of a particular CaMKII holoenzyme.
source: Since CaMKII holoenzymes are anchored within the post-synaptic density, the differences in the lengths of the kinase-hub linkers in different isoforms may likewise control the spatial extent of substrate phosphorylation enabled by the activation of a particular CaMKII holoenzyme.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional significance of linker length differences.

claim: The kinase-hub linker length in CaMKII can control the activation status of the holoenzyme, not just the spatial range of the kinase.
source: Our work has now revealed a key difference between CaMKII and AKAP:PKA complexes, which is that the kinase-hub linker length in CaMKII can control the activation status of the holoenzyme, not just the spatial range of the kinase.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the work comparing CaMKII to AKAP:PKA complexes.

claim: The protection afforded to pThr 286 is released by the addition of Ca2+/CaM.
source: The protection afforded to pThr 286 is released by the addition of Ca2+/CaM, suggesting that the calmodulin-binding element of CaMKII adopts a conformation that protects pThr 286 in the absence of Ca2+/CaM.
evidence: This is a result from dephosphorylation experiments with Ca2+/CaM.

claim: The observed resistance of pThr 286 to rapid dephosphorylation by phosphatases can enable CaMKII activity to persist for some time after the decay of Ca2+ pulses.
source: The observed resistance of pThr 286 to rapid dephosphorylation by phosphatases can enable CaMKII activity to persist for some time after the decay of Ca2+ pulses.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the dephosphorylation results.

claim: CaMKII subunits that are phosphorylated on Thr 286 have higher affinity for Ca2+/CaM, which can facilitate the rebinding of Ca2+/CaM during subsequent pulses of calcium.
source: In addition, CaMKII subunits that are phosphorylated on Thr 286 have higher affinity for Ca2+/CaM, which can facilitate the rebinding of Ca2+/CaM during subsequent pulses of calcium.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on known properties of CaMKII.

claim: Due to the cooperativity of Ca2+/CaM binding to CaMKII, a priming mechanism enables CaMKII holoenzymes that have retained some activating phosphorylation to rapidly reacquire higher levels of phosphorylation, even in the presence of subthreshold concentrations of Ca2+/CaM.
source: Due to the cooperativity of Ca2+/CaM binding to CaMKII, such a priming mechanism enables CaMKII holoenzymes that have retained some activating phosphorylation to rapidly reacquire higher levels of phosphorylation, even in the presence of subthreshold concentrations of Ca2+/CaM.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the priming experiments.

claim: The history of synaptic activity, including the frequency and the gaps between periods of activity, may be encoded in CaMKII.
source: This may enable the history of synaptic activity, including the frequency and the gaps between periods of activity, to be encoded in CaMKII.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation of the results.

claim: There are differences in the expression levels of CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β in neurons and these levels can be regulated by synaptic activity.
source: There are differences in the expression levels of CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β in neurons and these levels can be regulated by synaptic activity (Thiagarajan et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a known property of CaMKII expression supported by a citation.

claim: Differences in expression levels of CaMKII isoforms can result in differences in cellular targeting and stimulus frequency responses.
source: Differences in these levels can result in differences in cellular targeting and stimulus frequency responses (De Koninck and Schulman, 1998; Shen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a known property of CaMKII supported by citations.

claim: Expression level differences between isoforms can result in changing the balance of activating and inhibitory autophosphorylation.
source: We now show that expression level differences between isoforms can also result in changing the balance of activating and inhibitory autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the work on mixed holoenzymes.

claim: Autophosphorylation of the inhibitory site reduces binding of CaMKII-α to the postsynaptic density (PSD) in vitro.
source: Autophosphorylation of the inhibitory site reduces binding of CaMKII-α to the postsynaptic density (PSD) in vitro (Strack et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a known property of CaMKII supported by a citation.

claim: Abrogation of inhibitory autophosphorylation greatly reduces dissociation of the kinase from PSD in neurons.
source: By contrast, abrogation of such autophosphorylation greatly reduces dissociation of the kinase from PSD in neurons (Shen and Meyer, 1999) and increases PSD binding in transgenic animals, thereby altering synaptic plasticity and long-term potentiation (Elgersma et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a known property of CaMKII supported by citations.

claim: The rapid inhibitory phosphorylation of CaMKII-β limits binding of Ca2+/CaM, which is required for dissociation of the kinase from F-actin.
source: The rapid inhibitory phosphorylation of CaMKII-β, on the other hand, limits binding of Ca2+/CaM, which is required for dissociation of the kinase from F-actin (Shen and Meyer, 1999; Wang et al., 2019), an important step in structural remodeling of the synapse (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation supported by citations.

claim: By varying the relative expression levels of α and β-isoforms, the cell can generate CaMKII heterooligomers with variable response to activating signals.
source: Our results show that by varying the relative expression levels of α and β-isoforms, the cell can generate CaMKII heterooligomers with variable response to activating signals, thereby fine-tuning the response of CaMKII to Ca2+ spike trains in the brain.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the work on mixed holoenzymes.

claim: The autophosphorylation pattern for CaMKII-β* is essentially the same as for CaMKII-β.
source: The autophosphorylation pattern for CaMKII-β* is essentially the same as for CaMKII-β.
evidence: This is a result from comparing CaMKII-β and CaMKII-β*.

claim: Each CaMKII-β* holoenzyme exhibits about 5-fold greater phosphorylation of Thr 305/306 than is the case for CaMKII-α.
source: Each CaMKII-β* holoenzyme exhibits about 5-fold greater phosphorylation of Thr 305/306 than is the case for CaMKII-α (Figure 3b-right), with about 95% of the CaMKII-β* holoenzymes showing detectable phosphorylation at pThr 305/306.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the single-molecule assay shown in Figure 3b.

claim: About 95% of the CaMKII-β* holoenzymes show detectable phosphorylation at pThr 305/306.
source: Each CaMKII-β* holoenzyme exhibits about 5-fold greater phosphorylation of Thr 305/306 than is the case for CaMKII-α (Figure 3b-right), with about 95% of the CaMKII-β* holoenzymes showing detectable phosphorylation at pThr 305/306.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the single-molecule assay shown in Figure 3b.

claim: CaMKII-β* shows a lower degree of activating phosphorylation on Thr 286 when compared to CaMKII-α.
source: CaMKII-β* also shows a lower degree of activating phosphorylation on Thr 286 when compared to CaMKII-α (Figure 3b-left).
evidence: This is a comparative result from the single-molecule assay shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The results for CaMKII-γ*, with the long linker, resemble those for CaMKII-β/CaMKII-β*.
source: The results for CaMKII-γ*, with the long linker, resemble those for CaMKII-β/CaMKII-β* (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from testing CaMKII-γ* shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The results for CaMKII-δ*, with the short linker, resemble those for CaMKII-α.
source: Likewise, the results for CaMKII-δ*, with the short linker, resemble those for CaMKII-α (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from testing CaMKII-δ* shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Linker length alone is an important determinant of phosphorylation outcome.
source: The sequences of the linkers in the four CaMKII isoforms are very different, and so these results suggest that linker length alone is an important determinant of phosphorylation outcome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion from testing multiple isoforms with different linker lengths.

claim: For CaMKII-β'E and CaMKII-β'E*, there is a decrease in inhibitory phosphorylation and a small increase in activating phosphorylation when compared to CaMKII-β.
source: For both these constructs, we see a decrease in inhibitory phosphorylation and a small increase in activating phosphorylation when compared to CaMKII-β (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–b).
evidence: This is a result from testing the splice variant CaMKII-β'E shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The autophosphorylation outcome for CaMKII-α* is similar to that for CaMKII-α.
source: The autophosphorylation outcome for CaMKII-α* is similar to that for CaMKII-α (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is a result from testing CaMKII-α* shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β can assemble into mixed holoenzymes containing both isoforms.
source: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β can assemble into mixed holoenzymes containing both isoforms (Bennett et al., 1983; Brocke et al., 1999; Thiagarajan et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a known property of CaMKII supported by citations.

claim: Treatment of pre-activated CaMKII-α with ATP led to robust phosphorylation of CaMKII-α on Thr 305/306, at levels comparable to that for CaMKII-β.
source: ATP treatment of pre-activated CaMKII led to robust phosphorylation of CaMKII-α on Thr 305/306, at levels comparable to that for CaMKII-β (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 (a-c)).
evidence: This is a result from experiments testing the ability of CaMKII-α to be phosphorylated at Thr 305/306 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
